stories.headline: Wall Street ends a record-setting week higher, even as bond yields climb past 5.2%
stories.dek: The S&P 500 rose 0.6% Friday and the Dow added 423 points; big bank earnings and an inflation report come next.
stories.caveman: On Friday, Oct. 9, U.S. stocks went up. The S&P 500 (a scoreboard of 500 big U.S. companies) rose 0.6% to 7,811, close to its all-time high from three days before. The Dow rose 0.8% and the Nasdaq rose 0.6%. For the week, the S&P 500 was up 1.2%. But other markets were nervous. The interest rate on 10-year U.S. government bonds rose to 5.24%, which is very high. Oil stayed above $100 a barrel. One reason stocks rose: President Trump said he would not attack Iran before next month's midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: When bond rates are high, borrowing gets more expensive for homes, cars and companies. Investors are watching this week's bank profit reports and a new inflation number to guess whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates again.
stories.camps: Optimists: company profits are expected to grow about 30% this quarter, led by tech and energy, so stocks have a reason to climb. Worriers: a 5%+ bond yield and $100 oil can slow the economy and squeeze ordinary families, even while stock owners do well.
stories.image_alt: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange

terms.explain: A stock index that tracks 500 large U.S. companies; people use it as the main scoreboard for the U.S. stock market.
The interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow money; it affects loan rates everywhere.
U.S. elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, mostly for Congress.
The few weeks when companies report how much money they made last quarter.

stories.headline: Six senators from both parties tell Trump to drop his plan to buy diesel from Russia
stories.dek: Trump says Putin will send millions of tons of diesel to cut fuel prices; critics say it hands Russia money for its war.
stories.caveman: Diesel is the fuel that trucks, ships and farm machines use. Its price is very high right now because of the war in the Gulf. On Friday, President Trump said he made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on a phone call: Russia will send more than 300,000 tons of diesel right away, then more and more, up to millions of tons. On Sunday, six senators — four Republicans (Collins, Murkowski, Tillis, Curtis) and two Democrats (Shaheen, Blumenthal) — said the government must 'immediately reverse course.' They said the White House did not ask Congress first, which the law requires, and that buying Russian fuel gives Putin money while Russia keeps killing Ukrainian civilians.
stories.why_it_matters: Western countries have used sanctions to cut Russia's oil money since it invaded Ukraine. A U.S. deal to buy Russian fuel would be a big change and could weaken that pressure.
stories.camps: Supporters of the deal: more fuel means lower prices at the pump and for shipping goods, which helps working families now. Opponents in both parties: it rewards Russia's invasion, breaks with allies, and skipped the legal check by Congress.
stories.image_alt: President Donald Trump speaks with reporters after arriving on Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., Oct. 10, 2026

terms.explain: A heavy fuel used by trucks, buses, ships and machines.
Penalties, like trade bans, that countries put on another country to pressure it.
Supported by both major U.S. parties, Democrats and Republicans.
Change direction; undo a decision.

stories.headline: Oil posts a weekly gain as Hurricane Isaias shuts much of U.S. Gulf oil production
stories.dek: Brent crude settled at $104.72 a barrel; about 63% of U.S. Gulf output was shut before the storm.
stories.caveman: Oil is priced per barrel. Brent, the world's main oil price, ended Friday at $104.72, up 2.4% for the week. U.S. oil (WTI) ended at $91.85. Two things pushed prices up: fighting in the Middle East, which threatens ships near the Strait of Hormuz, and Hurricane Isaias, which forced oil companies on the U.S. Gulf coast to stop pumping. About 63% of U.S. Gulf oil production was shut before the storm. Prices dipped for a while on Friday after President Trump said he would not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil prices flow into everything: gasoline, plane tickets, plastic, food delivery. Long stretches of $100+ oil usually mean higher living costs around the world, hitting poorer countries hardest.
stories.camps: Some analysts: once the hurricane passes, U.S. production comes back and prices could ease. Others: the Gulf war and attacks on shipping are the bigger risk, so prices may stay high for a long time.
stories.image_alt: A Florida resident fills containers with petrol as he prepares for Hurricane Isaias
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via The National

terms.explain: The main world benchmark price for oil.
West Texas Intermediate, the main U.S. oil price.
The standard unit for oil: about 159 liters.
A narrow sea passage near Iran that a large share of the world's oil ships pass through.
When oil wells are turned off on purpose, for example before a storm.

stories.headline: AI memory boom gives Samsung a record $80 billion quarterly profit
stories.dek: Samsung estimates 107.4 trillion won in operating profit, up about 780% from a year ago — the first Korean company over 100 trillion won.
stories.caveman: Samsung, the giant South Korean company, makes phones, TVs and — most importantly right now — memory chips. AI computers need huge amounts of fast memory (like HBM and DRAM), and Samsung sells a lot of it. On Thursday it said it expects an operating profit of about 107.4 trillion won (around $80 billion) for July–September. That is about 8.8 times last year's number. Only Saudi Aramco, the oil giant, has made more in a single quarter. Samsung's phone and TV side was expected to lose money again, so almost all the gain came from chips.
stories.why_it_matters: This shows how much money the AI boom is moving into a few chip companies. It matters for Taiwan too: TSMC and Taiwanese memory and server makers ride the same wave.
stories.camps: Bulls: AI demand is so strong that chipmakers can raise prices. Skeptics: chip markets go in big boom-and-bust cycles, and if AI spending slows, memory prices can crash quickly.
stories.image_alt: A traffic light at Samsung Electronics headquarters in Suwon, South Korea
stories.image_credit: Photo: Yonhap via The Korea Times

terms.explain: Money a company makes from its main business, before taxes and interest.
A chip that stores data, like DRAM; AI needs lots of very fast memory.
High-bandwidth memory: stacked memory chips that feed data very fast to AI chips.
South Korea's currency.

stories.headline: OpenAI says its real yearly revenue is about $50 billion, not $68 billion — and AI stocks drop
stories.dek: Nvidia fell about 3%, Oracle about 5.5% and CoreWeave nearly 8% after the news on Oct. 8.
stories.caveman: OpenAI makes ChatGPT. Many reports said it was earning money at a pace of about $68–70 billion a year. But OpenAI told investors the cleaner number is about $50 billion; the bigger figure counted money that partners collect before paying OpenAI its share. That sounds like accounting, but investors got nervous, because many companies have promised to spend hundreds of billions of dollars building data centers for OpenAI. Shares of Nvidia, Oracle and CoreWeave fell on Thursday.
stories.why_it_matters: Huge AI spending is a big reason the stock market has been at records. If AI companies earn less than people hoped, the whole AI building boom — and the chip orders that help Taiwan — could slow.
stories.camps: Bulls: $50 billion a year is still enormous growth for a young company, and no actual sales were lost. Bears: the gap shows hype in AI numbers, and companies with lots of debt tied to OpenAI are risky.
stories.image_alt: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks at the company's developer conference, Sept. 29, 2026
stories.image_credit: Photo: Andrej Sokolow / Picture Alliance / Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A guess at a full year's sales, based on the current pace.
A huge building full of computers that run apps and AI.
A company that rents out AI computing power.
Gross is the total money collected; net is what's left after paying partners or costs.

stories.headline: Most Americans say AI is developing too fast, AP-NORC poll finds
stories.dek: 64% say 'too fast'; about 8 in 10 want the government to keep AI under human control and protect workers.
stories.caveman: A poll asked about 2,140 U.S. adults how they feel about artificial intelligence. 64% said AI is moving 'too fast,' 27% said 'about right,' and only 8% said 'too slow.' About 8 in 10 said it is very important for the government to make sure AI stays under human control, and almost as many want the government to protect workers' jobs. Democrats worry more (76% say too fast) than Republicans (54%), but worry is high in both parties. President Trump has argued against slowing AI down, saying China could get ahead.
stories.why_it_matters: AI companies want fewer rules; the public mostly wants more care. With midterm elections close, and fights over noisy, power-hungry data centers in many towns, AI is becoming a voting issue.
stories.camps: Pro-speed side: slowing down could let China lead and cost the U.S. jobs and power. Pro-caution side: AI is already changing jobs, power bills and safety, and voters want guardrails before it goes further.
stories.image_alt: AP-NORC poll on artificial intelligence

terms.explain: A survey that asks a sample of people their opinions.
A polling partnership between the Associated Press and NORC at the University of Chicago.
Rules or limits that keep something from going off track.
Shared by both major U.S. parties.

stories.headline: Nvidia is reportedly in talks to buy, or pour more money into, AI startup Reflection AI
stories.dek: Options include a full purchase, a bigger stake, or an 'acquihire' that would likely avoid long antitrust reviews.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that power most AI. Reflection AI is a startup that builds 'open-weight' AI models — models whose inner settings anyone can download and use. The Financial Times reported Nvidia is in early talks to either buy Reflection, invest more (it has already put in about $800 million), or do an 'acquihire': hire its people and license its tech without officially buying the company. A deal could come within weeks, but talks could also fall apart. Nvidia did a similar move with chip startup Groq last year and bought Hugging Face for $12.9 billion in September.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is using its huge profits to reach into more parts of AI. Fewer, bigger companies controlling AI raises questions about competition and prices.
stories.camps: Supporters: open models help more people use AI without paying a few big companies, and Nvidia's money speeds that up. Critics: 'acquihires' can be a way to swallow rivals while dodging the government's antitrust checks.
stories.image_alt: Reflection AI graphic

terms.explain: A young company trying to grow fast.
An AI model whose trained settings are released so others can run and change it.
Hiring a company's team (and licensing its tech) instead of buying the whole company.
Laws that stop companies from getting too much power over a market.

stories.headline: Four astronauts splash down after eight months in space; France's Sophie Adenot sets a European record
stories.dek: SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian crew home off Los Angeles after a delayed handover.
stories.caveman: Four astronauts came home from the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday, Oct. 8. A SpaceX capsule splashed into the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles. The crew — NASA's Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France's Sophie Adenot and Russia's Andrey Fedyaev — went up in February in a hurry, to replace a crew sent home early when NASA astronaut Mike Fincke got sick (NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years). Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs. Adenot's 237 days in orbit set a record for the European Space Agency.
stories.why_it_matters: The ISS is a rare place where the U.S. and Russia still work together. NASA depends on private company SpaceX to fly astronauts, which shows how much space travel now relies on one businessman's company.
stories.camps: Fans: private rockets made space trips cheaper and more regular. Worriers: relying so much on SpaceX gives Elon Musk's company a lot of power over a public program.
stories.image_alt: The SpaceX Crew Dragon Freedom splashes down in the Pacific off California, Oct. 8, 2026
stories.image_credit: Photo: Keegan Barber / NASA via AP

terms.explain: A big lab orbiting Earth, run by the U.S., Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada.
When a space capsule lands in the ocean.
The path something takes as it circles a planet.
Sending someone home early because of a health problem.

stories.headline: Trump announces a Russia–Ukraine 'energy ceasefire,' but Kyiv says Russian attacks kept coming
stories.dek: Zelenskyy welcomed the idea, then reported a Kharkiv power plant hit after the announcement.
stories.caveman: Russia has spent much of its 4½-year invasion bombing Ukraine's power plants, so people lose heat, light and water in winter. On Sunday, President Trump posted that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an 'energy ceasefire' — meaning they stop attacking each other's power systems — starting right away: 'Do not break it!' He gave no details, and Russia did not comment. Ukraine's President Zelenskyy called it good news and said Ukraine would stop hitting Russian energy sites if Russia did the same. But he said Russian drones and bombs kept striking that day, including a power plant in Kharkiv after Trump's post.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter is coming. If power attacks stop, millions of Ukrainians could stay warm. If the deal is only words, it may hurt trust in future peace talks.
stories.camps: Hopeful view: even a small, limited ceasefire can save lives and open the door to bigger talks. Skeptical view: no written terms, no checking system, and attacks right after the announcement suggest it isn't real yet. Trump has also blamed Zelenskyy for high U.S. diesel prices, which worries Ukraine's supporters.
stories.image_alt: A rescue worker puts out a fire at homes destroyed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine, Oct. 11, 2026

terms.explain: An agreement to stop fighting, sometimes only partly or for a time.
Power plants, power lines, gas pipes and other systems that deliver energy.
An Iranian-designed attack drone Russia uses in large numbers.
Ukraine's second-largest city, near the Russian border.

stories.headline: Poland arrests a man accused of plotting to kill Prime Minister Donald Tusk and the defense minister
stories.dek: Officials called the threat 'deadly serious'; the suspect, a Polish national, was detained in Lower Silesia.
stories.caveman: Donald Tusk is Poland's prime minister (the head of government). On Sunday, Polish police said they got believable information about planned attacks on Tusk and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Security officials held an emergency meeting. Soon after, police arrested a Polish man in the Lower Silesia region in the southwest. A spokesman said there was 'a strong likelihood' the threats could have been carried out. Reports say the man is about 60 and was active in radical online groups. Tusk thanked police for their 'swift and decisive action.'
stories.why_it_matters: Violence and threats against politicians are rising across Europe and the U.S. Poland is a key NATO country bordering Ukraine, and political attacks there can shake the whole region.
stories.camps: Government supporters: fast police action shows the system works. Critics of polarization: very angry online politics — from many sides — can push people toward violence, and leaders should cool the language.
stories.image_alt: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk

terms.explain: The head of government in many countries, like Poland or the U.K.
Murdering an important person, usually for political reasons.
A military alliance of North American and European countries that promise to defend each other.
Holding extreme views and wanting drastic change.

stories.headline: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says it is 'clear' Russia meddled in the 2016 Brexit vote
stories.dek: It is believed to be the first time a British leader has said so publicly; he warns Germany and France face the same threat.
stories.caveman: In 2016, British voters chose to leave the European Union — called Brexit. For years people asked whether Russia secretly tried to push the result. Andy Burnham became prime minister in July. In a podcast released Sunday, he said he asked his advisers, and 'I've had the clear answer that yes, there was' interference. He said saying it out loud helps voters in Germany and France understand that some politics there is pushed by enemies like Russia. Russia denies meddling in other countries' votes.
stories.why_it_matters: If foreign governments can quietly steer big votes, democracy is in danger. The comments come as British spies warn of growing Russian interference, and as far-right parties gain ground in Europe.
stories.camps: Supporters: naming the problem is the first step to protecting elections. Critics: some Brexit supporters say this is a way to question a fair democratic result; they want the evidence made public, not just a statement.
stories.image_alt: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks in Manchester, Oct. 9, 2026
stories.image_credit: Photo: Christopher Furlong / Pool via AP

terms.explain: Britain's exit from the European Union, decided by a 2016 vote.
A group of 27 European countries that share trade rules and many laws.
Secretly trying to influence another country's politics or elections.
A vote where all citizens decide one question directly.

stories.headline: Riyadh airport terminal hit again a day after a missile attack killed 12
stories.dek: Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed the strikes; Trump says he is weighing joining the fight against them.
stories.caveman: Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, has a big airport, King Khalid International. On Saturday a missile hit a domestic terminal there, killing 12 people and wounding about 300 — the deadliest attack on a Gulf Arab country since the Iran war began. On Sunday a projectile struck the same terminal again, causing a fire and more injuries. An Indian worker hurt on Saturday later died, raising the toll to 13. The Houthis, a rebel group in Yemen backed by Iran, said they did it. A Saudi-led coalition is fighting them. The airport was closed Sunday, and another airport in Dammam was also attacked.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a new, dangerous front in the war. Attacks on airports hurt ordinary travelers and workers — many of them migrant workers from Asia — and could pull the U.S. deeper into fighting.
stories.camps: Hawks: the U.S. should help Saudi Arabia strike back to stop more attacks. Doves: more U.S. bombing could widen the war, and Yemen's civilians have already suffered years of hunger and war; diplomacy should come first.
stories.image_alt: Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport after an attack

terms.explain: An armed rebel group that controls much of Yemen and is backed by Iran.
A group of countries working together, here in a military fight.
Anything fired through the air, like a missile or drone.
The part of an airport for flights inside the same country.

stories.headline: Anne Carson wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
stories.dek: The Canadian poet, 76, was honored for 'bold and inventive' work that mixes ancient Greek classics with modern life.
stories.caveman: The Nobel Prize in Literature is the most famous book prize in the world. It is given for a writer's whole body of work. On Oct. 8, the Swedish Academy picked Anne Carson, a 76-year-old poet, essayist and translator from Toronto. She also taught ancient Greek and Latin for over 30 years. Her books break the usual rules: 'Autobiography of Red' is a novel told in poems; 'Nox' is a grief book made like a scrapbook for her late brother; she also translated ancient Greek poets and worked with musicians like Laurie Anderson and Lou Reed. When the Academy called, she was in Iceland, 'listening to the wind.' The prize is about $1.2 million.
stories.why_it_matters: Carson isn't American, but she is huge in U.S. poetry and teaching, and her books are about to sell out across American bookstores. This week, she is the hottest name in literature.
stories.camps: Fans: she shows poetry can be fun, strange and deeply emotional, and she inspired a generation of writers. Doubters: her work can feel hard and academic, and some hoped the prize would go to a writer from a region the Nobel often overlooks, like Africa or Asia.
stories.image_alt: Anne Carson performs her work 'Antigonick' at the Moderna Museet in Stockholm, May 8, 2015
stories.image_credit: Photo: Pontus Lundahl / TT News Agency via AP

terms.explain: A yearly prize from the Swedish Academy for an author's lifetime of writing.

stories.headline: HOT: Rebecca Yarros's 'Threshing Day' sells 857,802 print copies in week one — 2026's biggest debut
stories.dek: The 'Fourth Wing' author's new short-story collection is already the third-best-selling book of the year.
stories.caveman: Rebecca Yarros wrote 'Fourth Wing,' a hugely popular 'romantasy' series (romance plus fantasy, with dragons). Her new book, 'Threshing Day,' is a collection of 13 stories set in the same world. In its first week, it sold 857,802 printed copies in the U.S., according to the sales tracker Circana BookScan. Only two books have sold more all year — Allen Levi's 'Theo of Golden' and Andy Weir's 'Project Hail Mary' — and those have been on sale since January.
stories.why_it_matters: Romantasy fans, many of them young women who share picks on TikTok, are now one of the strongest forces in U.S. publishing. Their buying power decides which books get made.
stories.camps: Fans: these books get millions of people excited about reading again. Critics: publishers chase the same trend too hard, and quieter literary books get less shelf space and attention.
stories.image_alt: Cover of 'Threshing Day' by Rebecca Yarros
stories.image_credit: Image: Red Tower Books via Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: A book genre that mixes romance and fantasy.
A first appearance; here, a book's first week of sales.
A service that counts how many printed books are sold in U.S. stores.
The book-loving community on TikTok that can turn titles into bestsellers.

stories.headline: HOT: Audrey Niffenegger returns with 'Life Out of Order,' a political sequel to 'The Time Traveler's Wife'
stories.dek: It took her 14 years; the new book follows Henry and Clare's time-traveling daughter, Alba, in a darker American future.
stories.caveman: In 2003, Audrey Niffenegger's first novel, 'The Time Traveler's Wife,' became a giant hit (over 9 million copies). It's a love story about Clare and Henry, a man who jumps through time without control. Her long-awaited sequel, 'Life Out of Order,' follows their daughter Alba, who has the same condition but more control — and uses it for personal and political goals. Niffenegger started it in 2012, when U.S. politics felt 'rosy.' Over 14 years, the scary futures she imagined, including neo-Nazis at a house party, began to look real. She told The Guardian, 'People forgot I existed.'
stories.why_it_matters: Big-name sequels decades later are a trend, and this one speaks to American worries about democracy and the far right.
stories.camps: Excited readers: a beloved world is back, with something urgent to say. Cautious readers: long-delayed sequels often disappoint, and some fans just want romance, not politics.
stories.image_alt: Audrey Niffenegger at her home in Chicago

terms.explain: A book that continues an earlier story.
Describing a scary, broken future society.

Feeling like a fake who doesn't deserve your success.

stories.headline: HOT: Min Jin Lee's 'American Hagwon' climbs the bestseller charts, nearly 10 years after 'Pachinko'
stories.dek: The 600-plus-page family epic follows Korean-born kids raised in New Jersey and Seoul, and the pressure of 'cram school' education.
stories.caveman: Min Jin Lee wrote 'Pachinko,' a famous novel about a Korean family in Japan. Her new book, 'American Hagwon,' took almost 10 years. A 'hagwon' is a Korean after-school cram school. The story follows the Koh family from 1992 to 2007: three kids born in New Jersey, moved to Australia and Korea, then back to America after a betrayal at the father's job. It asks: what does chasing a 'better future' through education cost a family? NPR called it sweeping and hard to put down. Some reviewers say parts are too long or preachy. It showed up as a new entry on hardcover bestseller charts this week.
stories.why_it_matters: Stories about immigrant families and education pressure are close to many readers' lives — in America, Korea and Taiwan alike.
stories.camps: Fans: deep, kind characters and a big look at immigration and class. Critics: at 600+ pages, it sprawls, and the school plot can drag.
stories.image_alt: Cover of 'American Hagwon' by Min Jin Lee

terms.explain: A private after-school 'cram school' in South Korea.

stories.headline: At least 139 migrants, including children, die after an overcrowded boat sinks off Djibouti
stories.dek: The boat carried more than 300 people; many victims were buried without names.
stories.caveman: Djibouti is a small country in East Africa, across the sea from Yemen. Many poor migrants, mostly from Ethiopia and Somalia, cross this route hoping to reach Saudi Arabia for work. On the evening of Oct. 8, a boat with more than 300 people sank soon after leaving, close to shore, mainly because it was overcrowded. The U.N. migration agency (IOM) said at least 139 people died, including children — and that only counts bodies buried by officials. 'They were buried with no names, in a common grave,' an IOM official said. Survivors are getting medical and mental-health help.
stories.why_it_matters: This route is one of the deadliest in the world but gets little attention. Poverty, war and climate stress push people to take huge risks.
stories.camps: Aid groups: create safe, legal work routes and stop smugglers who pack boats. Governments on the route: they want to stop smuggling, but critics say crackdowns alone push migrants to even more dangerous paths.
stories.image_alt: Authorities respond after a migrant boat capsized near Obock, Djibouti, Oct. 11, 2026
stories.image_credit: Photo: Alexandre Coissac / IOM via AP

stories.headline: Pope Leo calls the death penalty 'inadmissible' as the U.S. plans to livestream a firing-squad execution
stories.dek: The first American pope spoke on World Day Against the Death Penalty; the Pentagon plans to stream the Fort Hood shooter's execution.
stories.caveman: Pope Leo XIV, the leader of the Catholic Church and the first pope from the U.S., posted on Saturday that the death penalty is 'inadmissible' — not acceptable — because it attacks human dignity. He said societies can keep people safe with prisons while still leaving room for change. Saturday was World Day Against the Death Penalty. Two days earlier, the U.S. Defense Department said it will livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009; it is set for Dec. 3. President Trump said he will make the final call on the livestream. A botched execution in Tennessee has also renewed debate.
stories.why_it_matters: The U.S. is one of few rich democracies that still executes people. Showing an execution online would be a huge change in how punishment is seen.
stories.camps: Death penalty supporters: some crimes are so terrible that death is just, and victims' families deserve it. Opponents: innocent people have been executed, it is applied unequally by race and money, and broadcasting it makes violence a spectacle.
stories.image_alt: Pope Leo XIV arrives to celebrate Mass in St. Peter's Basilica, Oct. 8, 2026

terms.explain: When the government kills someone as punishment for a crime.

Showing video live on the internet.

stories.headline: Hurricane Simon pounds Mexico's Pacific coast near Puerto Vallarta as a Category 4 storm
stories.dek: Forecasters warned of 'catastrophic' wind and dangerous storm surge for resorts and poorer hillside towns.
stories.caveman: A hurricane is a giant spinning storm with very strong winds and rain. Hurricane Simon hit Mexico's west coast on Sunday as a Category 4 (the scale goes to 5), with winds around 215 km/h. Its center moved along the coast toward Puerto Vallarta, a big tourist city. The worst was expected overnight into Monday. Experts worried most about people living just inland and uphill from the beach hotels, where many homes may not survive strong winds. Meanwhile, two other storms, Rachel and Isaias, were still dumping rain on the U.S.
stories.why_it_matters: Warmer oceans are helping storms grow stronger faster. Poorer neighborhoods usually suffer the most damage and take the longest to recover.
stories.camps: Climate scientists: warmer seas fuel stronger hurricanes, so cutting emissions and preparing coasts both matter. Local critics: tourism zones often get better protection and faster help than the working-class towns around them.
stories.image_alt: A National Guard member patrols the seawall as Hurricane Simon approaches Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, Oct. 11, 2026

terms.explain: A huge tropical storm with winds over 119 km/h; called a typhoon in Asia.
The second-strongest level on the hurricane scale (1–5).
Sea water pushed onto land by a storm's winds.
The U.S. government office that tracks hurricanes.

stories.headline: Villages evacuated as a landslide-dam burst sends a flash flood down Nepal's Budhi Gandaki river
stories.dek: At least five people are missing; houses, four bridges and part of a hydropower site were swept away.
stories.caveman: In the mountains of north-central Nepal, a landslide fell into the Budhi Gandaki river and blocked it like a dam. When that natural dam broke on Sunday, a sudden wall of water rushed down the valley. About three dozen houses and four bridges were destroyed, and a hydropower plant construction site was damaged. At least five people are missing. The army used helicopters and soldiers to rescue 49 people. Officials told villagers along the river to move to higher ground. Nepal already suffered deadly landslides earlier this month.
stories.why_it_matters: Mountain countries like Nepal face more floods as glaciers melt and rains get heavier. Poor villages near rivers have little protection.
stories.camps: Climate advocates: rich countries that caused most warming should pay to help places like Nepal adapt. Development critics: building dams and roads in fragile valleys can also make landslides worse, so projects need stricter checks.
